summary: Defines the base syntax for Certificate Management over CMS (CMC), a protocol for requesting and managing public key certificates. It provides an interface to certification services built on CMS and PKCS #10 and an enrollment protocol that can be used with those. It updated an earlier CMC specification and was later replaced by RFC 10002.

plainLanguage.summary: Getting a digital ID card means filling in a form and proving who you are. This defines the form and the steps for asking a certificate authority for one. It has since been replaced by RFC 10002.

subtitle: A protocol for asking a certification authority for certificates, proving you hold the key, and managing them afterwards, built on CMS.

tldr.problem: PKI deployments needed a standard interface to certification services based on CMS and PKCS #10, and an enrollment protocol that works for keys that can only encrypt and cannot sign.
tldr.mechanism: CMC defines Simple and Full PKI Requests and Responses, carried in CMS. A Full PKI Request holds certification requests plus controls that handle proof of identity, proof of possession, status, revocation and certificate retrieval, and it allows Registration Authorities in between.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5272 obsoleted RFC 2797 and moved transport and compliance details to companion documents. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 10002 and updated by RFC 6402.

sections.title: Goals of CMC
sections.content:
Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) defines the base syntax for a certificate management protocol that uses the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). It addresses two needs in the Internet PKI community: an interface to public key certification products and services based on CMS and PKCS #10, and a PKI enrollment protocol for encryption-only keys.

The protocol requirements shape the design. It is to build on existing CMS, PKCS #10 and CRMF specifications. It must support all enrollment operations in a single round-trip where possible, allow all key generation on the client, include Proof-of-Possession (POP) methods, support deferred and pending responses, and allow arbitrary chains of Registration Authorities (RAs) between requesters and Certification Authorities (CAs).

RFC 5272 revises RFC 2797 with a major overhaul of the layout. Transport details moved to a separate document, and compliance requirements to another. Several new controls were added.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of an office that hands out ID cards. The aim is a form that works in one visit when possible, lets you keep your own secret, and lets helper offices pass requests along.

sections.title: Requests and Responses
sections.content:
An enrollment is usually one round-trip: a PKI Request from client to server and a PKI Response back. Delayed issuance needs more. There are two request types and two response types.

  • Simple PKI Request: a bare PKCS #10 certification request. It cannot carry proof of identity or any advanced service, and it needs a key that can sign.
  • Full PKI Request: one or more PKCS #10, CRMF or other request messages inside a PKIData structure, wrapped in a CMS SignedData or AuthenticatedData. A server MUST return a PKI Response to it.
  • Simple PKI Response: a certificates-only SignedData.
  • Full PKI Response: a PKIResponse content type inside a SignedData, used when more than certificates is returned, or the enrollment is pending or failed.

There is no special service for renewal or rekey: those look like any certification request, except the identity proof comes from an existing certificate from a trusted CA. The specification makes no assumption about transport, and the use of CMS does not imply email.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a quick form that only says who you are and what key you have, and a longer form with extra pages for special requests. The office answers with either just your new ID or an ID plus notes.

sections.title: Controls and Proof of Possession
sections.content:
Controls are the extra instructions carried in Full PKI Requests and Responses. Each is a unique object identifier (OID) followed by its data, and they are all defined under the id-cmc arc. Examples are status information (id-cmc-statusInfoV2), identity proof, transaction ID and nonces, revocation requests, get certificate and get CRL, query pending, and publishing trust anchors.

Status uses the CMCStatus values success, failed, pending, noSupport, confirmRequired, popRequired and partial. A failure can add a CMCFailInfo code such as badAlg, badRequest or tryLater.

Servers want proof that the requester holds the private key. For signing keys, signing the request is the POP. For encryption-only keys POP MUST be done by making the client decrypt a value, which cannot happen in one round-trip. It takes four steps: the client sends the public key, the server sends an encrypted challenge, the client sends back the decrypted plaintext, and the server validates it and continues.
sections.plainLanguage: To prove a key is yours, the office locks a note with your key's lock and asks you to read it back. Only the real key holder can open it, but it takes extra back-and-forth.

sections.title: Registration Authorities
sections.content:
A Registration Authority sits between the end entity and the CA. To the end entity it looks like the CA, and to the CA it looks like a client. An RA can batch several requests together, perform challenge-response POP proofs, add certificate extensions, archive private key material, or route requests to different CAs.

When an RA receives a request, it can forward it unchanged, add a new wrapping layer, or remove existing layers and add a new one. The new layer is a new PKIData that holds RA-added controls and the original client request. With several RAs on the path, requests acquire several layers.

An RA MUST NOT alter any certification request (PKCS #10 or CRMF), because that would invalidate its signature and the POP. Encryption layers must be removed in some cases, for example if the CA has no recipient entry in the encryption layer. Signature layers should be removed only when an encryption layer must change or when a CA will not accept multiple RA signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper desk sits between you and the ID office. It can add notes to your form and put it in a bigger envelope, but it must never change what you wrote.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Replay protection through the sender and recipient nonce controls may be needed depending on the environment. If the CA keeps enough state, replays may be detectable without nonces, but developers of state-constrained clients are strongly encouraged to use them.

Archiving a signing key needs extreme care, because the holder could forge signatures. Shared secrets used for authentication should come from good random number generation, since user-chosen secrets allow dictionary attacks. Implementations should also check cryptographic parameters to avoid weak ones, and the RFC names the small subgroup attack.

The Publish Trust Anchors control must be processed carefully. Incorrect handling allows an attacker to change the set of trusted anchors and weaken security, which the RFC calls slamming. Finally, a MAC in AuthenticatedData gives integrity but not authentication in all cases, so SignedData should be used instead when possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Several things can go wrong: someone replaying an old request, a stolen backup of a key, a guessable password, or someone slipping in a bad list of trusted offices. The RFC lists ways to guard against each.
